answer: The submission is candid and well structured, but several fixes would make it more credible and persuasive. (1) Fix the unit economics and internal inconsistencies. The 12 percent fee on $140 is $16.80, and net of 2.5 percent processing (applied to the full $156.80 billed, not just labor) the contribution is closer to $12.88 before background-check costs, support, and any payment-partner fixed fees. Show a full per-shift cost stack. Also reconcile traction math: 37 shifts and $622 in fees implies about $16.80 per shift, matching the model, but 5,180 labor spend over 37 shifts is exactly $140, which looks suspiciously uniform; explain whether this is real data or rounded. (2) Stress-test the 40 shifts per month per caterer assumption. Your only client did 37 shifts in six weeks (about 25 per month), and with 12 caterers the stated 1,800 shifts per month implies 150 per caterer, which contradicts the 40-shift assumption and the 20-person client's actual usage. Reconcile the projection (12 caterers x 40 = 480 shifts, not 1,800, and $30,000 monthly revenue would need about 1,800 shifts at $16.80) or explain what drives the gap. Right now the headline projections do not follow from the stated assumptions. (3) Rebuild the market sizing. The 120,000-shift estimate rests on assumptions (60 events, 8 roles each, all 250 caterers) that look high for small and mid-sized caterers and are untested; present a bottom-up range with low, base, and high cases and state the realistic serviceable share rather than the whole metro labor spend. The national extrapolation by population adds little and should be cut or heavily caveated. (4) Present evidence of willingness to pay and retention, not just pain. The 31 interviews show the problem exists, but not that caterers will pay a 12 percent fee on top of labor versus free group texts or 30 to 50 percent agency markups. Report the price reactions from interviews, the first client's repeat-use curve, whether they would be disappointed to lose it, and worker-side metrics such as acceptance rate, no-show rate, and repeat workers (60 of 140 completed a shift is a useful stat to analyze). (5) Address the cold-start and disintermediation risk directly. Caterers can use the platform to find workers once and then go around you; explain what prevents this (instant payment, ratings, insurance, compliance records) and how you will keep both sides dense enough to hit above 90 percent fill. Quantify your current fill rate rather than only average fill time. (6) Treat worker classification and payments compliance as a core section, not a closing risk note. Specify whether workers are independent contractors or W-2 via a partner, who bears payroll taxes, workers' comp, and liability for no-shows or incidents, and how instant pay is licensed and funded (float risk on paying workers before billing caterers). Name the payments partner and the cost of capital or chargeback exposure. This is the most likely threat to the model and investors will look for it first. (7) Tighten the competitive analysis with named competitors and a comparison table. Naming real players in event and hospitality staffing and showing concretely where you win (speed, price, roster feature) is stronger than category descriptions. The claim that local density is the moat should be supported with a plan for how many workers per caterer you need and how fast you can add them. (8) Make the ask and plan more specific. Break the $25,000 into a line-item budget with milestones by month, show runway given the $11,000 remaining and burn, and define pilot success metrics beyond six repeat caterers and 90 percent fill (for example shifts per caterer per month, contribution margin, worker retention). Clarify what happens if the award is not won. (9) Strengthen the team section. Equal founder equity is fine but state vesting and roles; the lack of an advisor on labor compliance is a gap you identify yourself, so name a target advisor or show outreach already underway. Also note that the CEO's banquet experience is a strength worth tying to specific insights that shaped the product. (10) Presentation: lead the executive summary with the single strongest proof point (37 shifts filled in 5.5 hours average, paid customer) and a one-line value proposition, cut hedging language that repeats 'rough' and 'we regard as targets' in several sections, and consolidate the assumptions into one clear table so reviewers can see what is observed versus assumed.
